headline: Approved memorandum of understanding between the city's Office of Youth Services and the school district.
summary: Residents raised traffic safety near Jewett Street School and school cleaning concerns. The meeting also covered enrollment, class sizes, bus driver shortages, and a tuition obligation estimated at $240,000 for fifteen students attending Granite State Academy.
decisions: Approved the memorandum of understanding between the Office of Youth Services and the Manchester School District, all in favor.
Approved the balance personnel report and supplemental report as submitted, all present in favor.
Approved item 19 from the personnel report, all in favor, after the item was discussed in non-public session.
Seated Committee Member Stewart as a Pro-Tem Member of the Finance and Facilities committee until new members are seated.

On motion of Committee Member Turner, duly seconded by Committee Member Want, it was moved to approve item 19 from the Personnel report. All were in favor and the motion passed.

BOARD OF SCHOOL COMMITTEE 
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
 
TUESDAY, October 13, 2026 6:30 p.m.  
 
1. Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. 
 
2. Mayor Ruais called for the Pledge of Allegiance. 
 
Mayor Ruais welcomed Principal Muncey and students from Gossler Park Elementary School to 
lead the Pledge of Allegiance. Committee Members Hamer and O’Neil-Wong introduced the 
students: 
 
Gossler Park Elementary School – Principal Sarah Muncey 
 
Myla Diaz – Grade 2   Kobe Diaz – Grade 3  Ward 10 
James Plourde – Grade 4  Hazel Plourde – Grade 3 Ward 11 
 
3. A moment of silence was observed.  
 
A moment of silence was observed. Vice Chairman O'Connell requested that the Board remember 
Committee Member Sean Parr and his family following the recent passing of his mother. 
 
4. The Clerk calls the roll.  
 
Present:  Committee Members Turner, Georges, Want, Taylor, Stewart, 
O’Connell, St. John, Garrity, Hamer, O’Neil-Wong, Smith and Mayor 
Ruais. 
 
Absent: Committee Member Parr was absent.  Committee Member Bergeron 
resigned.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 2 of 26 
 
5.       RECOGNITIONS 
 
a. Recognition of Committee Member Chris Potter for Five Years of Service to the 
Manchester Board of School Committee 
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell recognized Committee Member Chris Potter for five years of 
dedicated service to the Manchester Board of School Committee, the students and families of 
Manchester, and the greater community.  He shared that Committee Member Potter first came to 
Manchester in 2012 through City Year, beginning what would become a lasting commitment to 
the community. That commitment eventually led him to serve as the Ward 7 representative on 
the Board of School Committee, where he brought a thoughtful, engaged, and student-centered 
perspective to the Board's work.  Throughout his service, Committee Member Potter was 
actively involved in issues affecting students, staff, families, and schools. He served on various 
committees, including Finance and Facilities and Policy, where he consistently asked thoughtful 
questions, raised concerns, and worked to ensure that decisions considered both the immediate 
and long-term needs of the District.  Vice Chairman O'Connell highlighted Committee Member 
Potter's advocacy for improvements to school facilities, expanded student supports beyond the 
classroom, and efforts to reduce class sizes. He also acknowledged Committee Member Potter's 
attention to matters involving transportation, student discipline, language access for families, and 
ensuring opportunities for all students to succeed.  He further noted that, although Committee 
Member Potter and his family would be relocating outside Manchester, his commitment to the 
community and its future remained strong.  
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell emphasized the significant time and dedication required of public 
servants, including evenings away from family, countless documents to review, difficult 
discussions, and important decisions. He thanked Committee Member Potter for willingly 
making that commitment over the past five years and wished him and his family the very best. 
 
Committee Member Want added her appreciation for Committee Member Potter's service, 
specifically recognizing his leadership and advocacy concerning the location of the new Beech 
Street School. Committee Member Want recalled that the new school had originally been 
proposed for the McDonough School site. She credited Committee Member Potter, along with
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 3 of 26 
 
former Committee Member Bonilla, for advocating that the Center City neighborhood needed a 
new school and that the Beech Street area was the more appropriate location. 
 
Committee Member Want stated that, although her own ward ultimately would not receive the 
new school, she believed the Board made the right decision. She emphasized that Committee 
Member Potter had been among the first to advocate publicly for the Beech Street location and 
that his efforts played an important role in the Board's decision. 
 
Committee Member Want thanked Committee Member Potter for his dedication and stated that 
he would be missed. 
 
PUBLIC FORUM – 6:38 P.M. 
 
6. The purpose of the public forum is to give the residents of Manchester the opportunity to 
address the board.  All people wishing to speak will have up to three (3) minutes to do so, 
and any comments must be directed to the chair.  Any resident wishing to speak will 
come forward to the nearest microphone, clearly state their name and address when 
recognized and give their comments.  
 
Speakers may offer comments on school operations and programs that concern them.  In 
public session, however, the Board shall not hear personal complaints of school personnel 
or complaints against any person connected with the District.  Other channels are 
provided for Board consideration and disposition of legitimate complaints involving  
school district employees, which should be referred to the Superintendent.  Speakers are 
requested to refrain from providing confidential information during this comment period.  
Any comments that are given regarding personnel matters, will not be responded to by 
the Board or Administration during the public meeting, as these items should be 
discussed in non-public session. 
 
Jessica Spillers – 73 Jobin Drive, stated: 
Jessica Spillers addressed the Board regarding concerns with traffic safety in the vicinity of 
Jewett Street School. Ms. Spillers explained that traffic conditions during student arrival and 
dismissal had become increasingly concerning. She noted that two crossing guards were 
generally present in the morning, with one positioned near the Cilley Road and Jewett Street 
intersection and another directly in front of the school. However, she indicated that afternoon 
coverage appeared to be limited to the crossing guard near Cilley Road.  She expressed concern
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 4 of 26 
 
that school staff members, including an individual she identified as Mr. V, were attempting to 
assist students crossing the street directly in front of the school. She reported observing vehicles 
failing to slow down or stop appropriately, creating potentially dangerous situations for students 
and staff.  Ms. Spillers also raised concerns about the limited number of clearly marked 
crosswalks, the positioning of flashing warning lights away from the immediate school area, and 
motorists making unsafe U-turns during pickup and drop-off periods.  She informed the Board 
that she had already brought these concerns to the Board of Mayor and Aldermen and hoped both 
bodies could work together to address the conditions before someone was injured.  Ms. Spillers 
also raised concerns regarding reports she had received that cleaning services in some District 
schools had been reduced, potentially to once per week, with teachers being asked to perform 
additional cleaning.  She questioned whether those reported changes were related to the Aramark 
contract and expressed concern about the implications for cleanliness, particularly as cold and flu 
season approached. She encouraged the Board to consider whether funding could be identified 
elsewhere to maintain appropriate cleaning services. 
 
a. If there is no one else present wishing to speak, a motion is in order to take all 
comments under advisement and further to receive and file any written 
documentation presented and to table the remaining minutes for public comment 
to the end of the meeting for those that have not already spoken. 
 
 
On motion of Committee Member Turner, duly seconded by Committee Member Want, it 
was moved to take all comments under advisement and further to receive and file any written 
documentation presented and to table the remaining minutes for public comment to the end 
of the meeting for those that have not already spoken.  All present were in favor and the 
motion passed. 
 
 
 
7. Response to Public Comment 
 
Committee Member Turner asked whether the Board of Mayor and Aldermen had discussed 
the traffic concerns near Jewett Street School. She noted that flashing crosswalk signals, such as 
the one near West High School, appeared to be effective and suggested exploring similar 
measures near Jewett Street School and on Beech Street near Central High School.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 5 of 26 
 
 
Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Chmiel indicated that she had not received an increase in complaints 
specifically regarding Jewett Street but acknowledged the longstanding traffic challenges around 
Jewett Street and Southside Middle Schools.  She explained that the District and City had 
completed multiple traffic studies in that area over the years and that the combination of schools, 
surrounding neighborhoods, and limited road access created significant congestion during arrival 
and dismissal. 
 
Dr. Chmiel stated that the District would bring Ms. Spillers' comments and the suggestion for 
additional flashing crosswalk signals to the appropriate City officials, including the traffic 
engineer, Department of Public Works, and Manchester Police Department's traffic division. 
She also explained that traffic patterns were being reviewed as part of the Southside Middle 
School renovation and addition project. Similar traffic concerns at other schools, including 
Weston, Northwest, and Hillside, continued to be evaluated in coordination with City 
departments. 
 
Committee Member Want recalled previous traffic concerns at Weston Elementary School, 
where increased police patrols during arrival and dismissal had helped improve safety. She 
suggested that the Manchester Police Department consider providing additional enforcement 
around Jewett Street School for several weeks to help address speeding and unsafe driving 
behaviors. 
 
Committee Member Smith asked whether temporarily restricting traffic in one direction along 
Jewett Street during dismissal could improve safety for students walking home.  Mayor Ruais 
acknowledged the suggestion but noted that road closures could create additional complications 
for surrounding neighborhoods. He recommended that the District and City continue working 
with Public Works, the traffic engineer, and the Manchester Police Department to review the 
concerns and identify potential solutions. 
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell added that the Southside Middle School renovation project would 
provide improvements to student drop-off and pickup operations. He explained that the project
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 6 of 26 
 
would allow some school buses, smaller buses, and vans to pull off the roadway, potentially 
reducing congestion along Jewett Street. 
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell also addressed Ms. Spillers' concerns regarding school cleaning. He 
stated that the District's revised Aramark contract was scheduled to be reviewed by the 
Committee on Finance and Facilities at its rescheduled meeting on Wednesday, October 21, 
2026.  He acknowledged that the revised contract reflected budget reductions and that the 
Committee would need to discuss the appropriate level of cleaning services, the associated costs, 
and what level of cleanliness was acceptable within the District's available resources. 
 
 
8.   PRESENTATIONS 
 
There were no presentations this evening. 
 
9. ACTION AGENDA 
 
a. Office of Youth Services and Manchester School District Memorandum    
of Understanding – by Mayor Jay Ruais, in conjunction with Attorney  
Matt Upton 
 
Mayor Ruais introduced the proposed Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the City 
of Manchester's Office of Youth Services and the Manchester School District. He acknowledged 
the work of Elaine Michaud from the Manchester Health Department, Executive Director of Safe 
and Supportive Schools Stacy Champey, Attorney Upton, and others involved in developing the 
agreement. 
 
On motion of Vice Chairman O'Connell, duly seconded by Committee Member Want, it was 
moved to approve the MOU. 
 
Mayor Ruais explained that the agreement resulted from a broader review of the Office of Youth 
Services and its operations. The review sought to identify ways to strengthen existing programs, 
clarify responsibilities, and improve collaboration between the City and the Manchester School
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 7 of 26 
 
District.  He stated that the MOU established clearer roles and responsibilities for the Office of 
Youth Services, particularly as they related to student attendance, truancy, and class cutting. 
The agreement also addressed communication between the City and District, mandated reporting 
responsibilities, data collection, and the sharing of progress information with both the Board of 
Mayor and Aldermen and the Board of School Committee. 
 
Mayor Ruais emphasized that the goal was to build on the important work already taking place 
while creating stronger coordination and accountability between the two entities. 
 
Committee Member Stewart commended Executive Director Stacy Champey for her recent 
presentation concerning the District's Multi-Tiered Systems of Support for Behavior (MTSS-B). 
She highlighted the extensive work being undertaken to establish meaningful behavioral supports 
for students and expressed appreciation that the City was partnering with the District to provide 
additional resources and support.  She asked whether a director for the Office of Youth Services 
had already been hired.  Mayor Ruais explained that following the resignation of the previous 
director, an interim director had been appointed. Rather than immediately filling the permanent 
position, the City chose to undertake a comprehensive evaluation of the department and its future 
needs.  He stated that updated job descriptions had been presented through the City's Human 
Resources process and were expected to be considered by the Board of Mayor and Aldermen. 
Once approved, the City would begin the hiring process. 
 
Committee Member Stewart also recognized the work completed over the summer by the City, 
Manchester Proud, and community partners in developing a broader understanding of youth 
services needs.  Mayor Ruais explained that multiple meetings had been held, involving more 
than 100 individual participants and representation from approximately 75 youth-serving 
organizations. Granite United Way and Manchester Proud subsequently presented findings to the 
Board of Mayor and Aldermen.  He further explained that Elaine Michaud completed an 
operational assessment over approximately six to eight weeks, which included staff interviews, 
community partner discussions, and an evaluation of opportunities to strengthen the department.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 8 of 26 
 
The combined work resulted in a 92-page report presented to the Board of Mayor and Aldermen. 
Mayor Ruais stressed that the proposed MOU was the result of considerable collaboration among 
City staff, District administration, community organizations, and other stakeholders. 
 
All were in favor and the motion passed. 
 
 
10. CONSENT AGENDA (ITEMS 10 – 17)  
 
a. Mayor Ruais advises if you desire to remove any of the following items from the 
Consent Agenda, please so indicate.  If none of the items are to be removed, only one 
motion will be taken at the conclusion of the presentation.  
 
There were no requests to remove items from the Consent Agenda. 
 
On motion of Vice Chairman O'Connell, duly seconded by Committee Member Turner, it was 
moved to approve the Consent Agenda. 
 
b. Approval of minutes from the Board of School Committee meetings on: September 
28, 2026. 
 
c. Report(s) of the Committee on Policy, if available.  
 
d. Report(s) of the Committee of Teaching and Learning, if available.   
 
e. Report(s) of the Committee of Finance and Facilities, if available.  
  
f. Report(s) of the Committee of Student Conduct, if available.  
 
g. Report(s) of the Committee on Education Legislation, if available.  
 
h. Report(s) of the Joint School Buildings Committee (City Committee).  
  
i. Special Committees, if applicable: 
 
o Report from the Special Committee on Athletics, if available.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee

COMMUNICATIONS 
 
11. Superintendent’s Communications.  
 
a) Superintendent Updates: 
 
Superintendent Dr. Jennifer Chmiel advised that a written memorandum had been distributed to 
Board Members and has been made available electronically to the public. The report included 
updates regarding enrollment, class sizes, athletics, personnel, recruitment, transportation, and 
open enrollment tuition obligations. 
 
District Enrollment 
Dr. Chmiel reported that, as of October 1, 2026, total District enrollment was 11,707 students, 
including preschool students and out-of-district students participating in Manchester School of 
Technology career and technical education programs.  Excluding those populations, the District's 
kindergarten through Grade 12 enrollment was 11,042 students, compared with 11,065 at the 
previous meeting, a decrease of 23 students. 
 
She noted that the District ended the previous school year with 11,053 K–12 students, meaning 
current enrollment was only 11 students below the previous year's ending enrollment.  She stated 
that overall enrollment remained relatively consistent with the prior year. However, the District 
would continue monitoring enrollment at individual schools and grade levels, particularly at the 
elementary level, where shifts in student populations could affect class sizes. 
 
Dr. Chmiel further advised that this would be the final enrollment presentation of this format, 
although monthly enrollment reports would continue to be provided to the Board, along with 
updates regarding significant changes in class sizes. 
 
Elementary School Enrollment and Class Sizes 
Assistant Superintendent Doherty reported that elementary class sizes remained generally 
consistent with the previous update.  She identified Gossler Park, Green Acres, Highland, Jewett, 
Smith, and Weston as schools with particular grade levels experiencing larger class sizes.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 10 of 26 
 
In response to previous requests from the Board, the District added two additional data points to 
its reporting: the number of students attending schools other than their assigned neighborhood 
school because of class size capacity, and the number of approved in-district transfer requests at 
each school and grade level. 
 
Assistant Superintendent Doherty explained that during the review of these additional data 
points, staff identified possible inconsistencies in how some information had been entered into 
the student information system.  She stated that the District was working with building 
administrators to verify the accuracy of the information and ensure that students placed outside 
their home schools due to capacity limitations were being reported correctly. She emphasized 
that while classroom space existed throughout the District, it was not always available in the 
neighborhoods or grade levels where students resided. This continued to present challenges in 
balancing class sizes while making every effort to keep students in their assigned neighborhood 
schools. 
 
She reported that the majority of elementary classrooms remained at or below the District's class 
size policy of 20 students and that the Administration would continue monitoring enrollment, 
verifying data, and making adjustments where possible. 
 
Middle School Enrollment and Class Sizes 
Assistant Superintendent Roth reported that current middle school enrollment totaled 3,274 
students in Grades 5 through 8.  He provided the following school-specific information: 
 Hillside Middle School: 963 students, with two classes exceeding 25 students, both in 
Grade 8, involving advanced art and algebra. 
 McLaughlin Middle School: 819 students, with several classes exceeding 25 students. 
Most of those classes had 26 or 27 students, with the largest concentration in unified arts, 
including music and art. 
 Middle School at Parkside: 743 students, with three classes exceeding 25 students, 
involving pre-algebra, physical education, and art.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 11 of 26 
 
 Southside Middle School: 749 students, with ten classes exceeding 25 students, all in 
Grade 8. These included two English language arts classes, two social studies classes, 
two mathematics classes, one science class, and three physical education classes. 
 
Assistant Superintendent Roth stated that most middle school classes remained at or below the 
District's class size policy of 25 students and that overall class sizes continued to be manageable. 
 
High School Enrollment and Class Sizes 
Assistant Superintendent Dr. Espinola reported that the District currently served 3,402 high 
school students across Central High School, Memorial High School, Manchester School of 
Technology High School, and West High School.  This total did not include the 244 students 
enrolled in Manchester School of Technology's career and technical education program. 
She reported that no significant changes had occurred in high school class sizes since the 
previous update: 
1. Central High School had four classes exceeding 25 students;  
2. Memorial High School had thirteen;  
3. West High School had eighteen, including three Algebra I classes with enrollments of 30 
students; and, 
4. Manchester School of Technology, 26 instructional or support classes remained above 
their listed maximums. 
 
Dr. Espinola emphasized that adjusting high school class sizes was particularly complex because 
individual student schedules involved multiple academic requirements, electives, lunch periods, 
and courses necessary for graduation.  She explained that moving a student from one class could 
create scheduling conflicts in other courses. The Administration continued working with high 
school principals to identify opportunities to address class sizes while ensuring students 
remained on track to meet graduation requirements.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 12 of 26 
 
Personnel and Recruitment 
Ms. Evans provided an update on District hiring and recruitment efforts.  She highlighted several 
recent hires, including one special education teacher for Central High School, one licensed 
nursing assistant, six paraprofessionals, and three registered behavior technicians.  She noted that 
the newly hired licensed nursing assistant represented the District's second directly employed 
LNA serving students. 
 
Ms. Evans explained that Human Resources was working closely with building administrators to 
develop targeted recruitment efforts, including social media campaigns, to address hard-to-fill 
positions.  Priority areas included special education teachers, bus drivers, crossing guards, and 
other critical staffing needs.  She also advised that official employee retention rates would be 
calculated once the District received the necessary state data, after which the information would 
be analyzed and shared with the Board. 
 
Athletics 
Dr. Espinola reported that the fall athletic season was approaching its conclusion at Manchester 
Central, Memorial, and West High Schools.  Student athletes and teams were preparing for their 
final regular-season competitions, with several programs working toward postseason 
opportunities.  She recognized the dedication and commitment demonstrated by student athletes, 
coaches, athletic directors, families, and supporters throughout the season and expressed the 
District's continued support for the teams as they pursued playoff opportunities. 
 
Home-to-School Transportation 
Dr. Espinola reported that regular home-to-school transportation continued to face challenges 
related to driver availability.  She explained that daily adjustments, substitute drivers, and route 
reassignments remained necessary to maintain transportation services. While some delays 
continued, the District remained focused on providing safe and reliable transportation while 
minimizing disruptions to students and families.  She reported a significant improvement in fleet 
availability. Of the District's 56 school buses, 49 were currently in service and seven were out of 
service, representing approximately 88 percent fleet availability.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 13 of 26 
 
Under the prior maintenance agreement, as many as eighteen buses had been unavailable at one 
time. Dr. Espinola attributed the improvement to more dedicated attention to fleet maintenance, 
faster repairs, and improved vehicle availability.  She stated that driver recruitment remained a 
priority and that the District was interviewing candidates, with the expectation that two 
candidates might be brought forward for consideration at the next Board meeting. 
 
Specialized Transportation 
Assistant Superintendent Roth reported that 842 students were actively receiving specialized 
transportation services.  He stated that the District was coordinating 89 buses and vans each day, 
supported by 89 drivers and 40 monitors.  He explained that the specialized transportation team 
continued managing frequent adjustments involving student schedules, addresses, school 
assignments, service requirements, and pickup and drop-off locations. 
 
School Start Times 
Dr. Espinola informed the Board that the school start time presentation originally scheduled for 
the meeting would instead be discussed during non-public session.  She explained that proposed 
adjustments to school bell times could affect existing negotiated agreements and ongoing 
collective bargaining discussions, making it appropriate to address those matters in non-public 
session. 
 
Open Enrollment Tuition 
Attorney Upton reported that the District had received notice of a tuition obligation related to 
Manchester students enrolled in an open enrollment school district. He explained that Prospect 
Mountain School District operated an alternative online program known as Granite State 
Academy.  During the previous school year, fifteen Manchester students participated in the 
program, and Prospect Mountain had elected not to charge the Manchester School District tuition 
for those students.  Following resolution of legal questions concerning open enrollment school 
districts by the New Hampshire Supreme Court, Prospect Mountain had decided to begin 
assessing tuition for participating students.  Attorney Upton reported that fifteen Manchester 
students were currently attending Granite State Academy.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 14 of 26 
 
He explained that under the applicable law, the resident school district was responsible for 
tuition equivalent to 80 percent of its average per-pupil cost.  Based on the estimated cost of 
approximately $16,000 per student, the District anticipated a tuition obligation of approximately 
$240,000 for the fifteen students. 
 
Attorney Upton stated that the District had been notified of the enrollment and expected to 
receive the actual invoice in December.  He indicated that any additional legal questions 
concerning the obligation could be addressed in non-public session. 
 
Manchester School of Technology Aviation Program and State of the District 
Dr. Chmiel congratulated Manchester School of Technology's Aviation Program on the ribbon-
cutting ceremony celebrating its second student-built airplane.  She clarified that the event, held 
on Saturday, October 10, 2026, had been organized by the Aviation Museum of New Hampshire 
rather than the Manchester School District.  She stated that the District had not been responsible 
for issuing invitations and had understood that members of the Board of School Committee and 
Board of Mayor and Aldermen would be included. 
 
Dr. Chmiel also thanked the Greater Manchester Chamber of Commerce and the District staff 
who helped organize the fifth annual State of the District event, held October 1, 2026, and 
expressed appreciation to the Board Members who attended. 
 
Comments and questions from the Board included: 
 
Committee Member Taylor thanked the Administration for providing additional data regarding 
students attending schools outside their assigned neighborhoods due to capacity constraints. 
He questioned why students were listed as displaced from certain schools when the enrollment 
reports appeared to show available classroom seats. He referenced Webster Elementary School's 
Grade 2 enrollment and kindergarten enrollment at Weston as examples. 
 
Assistant Superintendent Doherty explained that some students had originally been placed 
outside their assigned schools when classrooms were at capacity in earlier grades.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 15 of 26 
 
As those students progressed through school and spaces became available, parents were offered 
the opportunity to have their children remain in the schools they had already been attending, 
rather than requiring them to return to their neighborhood schools.   Regarding Weston, she 
explained that the District was working to increase inclusion opportunities for students in self-
contained special education programs. Certain kindergarten and first-grade seats were 
intentionally being maintained to allow those students to participate in general education 
classrooms without exceeding class size limits. 
 
Committee Member Taylor acknowledged that individual student circumstances and 
programming needs made the data more complex than simply comparing total enrollment with 
classroom capacity. 
 
Committee Member Taylor also asked whether the anticipated Granite State Academy tuition 
obligation resulted from the Board's earlier decision not to adopt an open enrollment policy. 
 
Dr. Chmiel confirmed that the Board had previously been presented with an opportunity to 
establish parameters governing students entering and leaving the District through open 
enrollment.  She explained that the Board had elected not to adopt such a policy and that the 
tuition obligation was one consequence of that decision. 
 
Committee Member Stewart asked Assistant Superintendent Doherty to clarify the concerns 
identified in the student placement data.  Assistant Superintendent Doherty explained that she 
had noticed several figures that appeared inconsistent with information provided by building 
principals.  She stated that staff were reviewing whether the data had been entered correctly into 
the student information system and were working to confirm the accuracy of the reports. 
 
Dr. Chmiel commended school principals, administrative assistants, and District leadership for 
improving the reliability of student information and for questioning data that did not appear 
accurate.  She explained that the District had made considerable progress in standardizing data 
entry procedures and improving the quality of reports generated through Aspen.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 16 of 26 
 
She noted that rather than simply accepting the information produced by the system, staff were 
comparing the figures with their knowledge of students and investigating potential discrepancies. 
Committee Member Stewart thanked the Administration for its attention to data accuracy and 
emphasized the importance of remembering that each enrollment figure represented an 
individual student with specific educational needs. 
 
Committee Member Stewart returned to the concerns raised during public comment regarding 
traffic safety around Jewett Street School.  She noted that the District currently had eight vacant 
crossing guard positions and questioned what additional recruitment measures were being 
pursued to fill those positions. 
 
Dr. Chmiel explained that the Administration was asking elementary school principals to 
promote crossing guard and bus driver openings through school communications, parent groups, 
and social media.  She stated that these positions could be attractive to parents and other 
community members because of the hours involved and encouraged Board Members and the 
public to help spread information about available positions. 
 
She also reiterated the District's ongoing recruitment needs for special education teachers, nurses, 
paraprofessionals, bus drivers, and crossing guards. 
 
Committee Member Stewart emphasized that keeping students safe was a responsibility shared 
by the entire community and encouraged interested residents to consider serving as crossing 
guards. 
 
Committee Member Hamer questioned whether requiring bus driver candidates to receive formal 
Board approval could create unnecessary delays in filling vacant positions.  He expressed 
concern that the District needed drivers immediately and should avoid losing qualified applicants 
while awaiting a scheduled Board meeting. 
 
Dr. Chmiel explained that bus drivers were non-certified employees and that she had conditional 
hiring authority for those positions.  She stated that this allowed the District to make conditional
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 17 of 26 
 
employment offers and begin the hiring process before final Board approval, helping to expedite 
recruitment.  She confirmed that the District was using that authority when appropriate to fill 
critical vacancies as quickly as possible. 
 
Committee Member Want suggested that the District consider opportunities for paraprofessionals 
to work additional hours as crossing guards before or after their regular school assignments. 
She noted that some paraprofessionals might welcome additional compensation and would 
already be familiar with the students they would be assisting. 
 
Dr. Chmiel explained that the District had previously negotiated a Memorandum of 
Understanding with the paraprofessional bargaining unit specifically to allow employees to take 
on crossing guard responsibilities.  However, she reported that no employees had elected to 
participate in the opportunity. 
 
Committee Member Want suggested that the District renew its efforts to promote the 
arrangement, particularly through direct conversations between principals and paraprofessionals 
who might be interested.  She suggested that a personal invitation from a principal could be more 
effective than simply distributing information about the MOU. 
 
Dr. Chmiel agreed that the Administration could remind principals of the opportunity and 
encourage them to raise it with employees who might be interested in additional hours. 
 
Committee Member Turner expressed appreciation for the Administration's transparency 
regarding transportation staffing challenges and recognized the important work of District bus 
drivers.  She raised concerns about student behavior on school buses and asked what procedures 
were available to drivers who experienced repeated behavioral problems or unsafe situations. 
She explained that drivers experiencing difficult routes should feel supported and have a clear 
process for addressing student behavior before the situation became so stressful that they 
considered leaving their positions.
October 13, 2026, Board of School Committee 
Page 18 of 26 
 
Dr. Chmiel reported that Dr. Espinola had recently facilitated a meeting with District bus drivers 
at the Welcome Center to discuss challenges, student behavior, and opportunities to improve the 
transportation experience.  She described the meeting as productive and commended drivers for 
approaching the discussion collaboratively and offering practical ideas for addressing student 
behavior. 
 
Dr. Espinola explained that meetings with bus drivers were intended to take place monthly and 
provide opportunities to discuss concerns, review procedures, and share successful strategies. 
She stated that the Administration had discussed the District's Multi-Tiered Systems of Support 
for Behavior and the importance of helping students understand expectations for safe and 
respectful conduct on school buses.  She also reported creating a video for elementary students to 
view during morning meetings that addressed appropriate behavior while riding school buses. 
 
Dr. Espinola explained that drivers had suggested positive reinforcement strategies, including 
recognizing students for appropriate behavior and offering incentives, such as allowing students 
to select music or playlists during their bus rides.  She further explained that formal procedures 
remained in place for addressing repeated or serious behavioral concerns.  Drivers could submit 
disciplinary referrals to transportation specialists, who would forward the information to the 
appropriate schools. School administrators would then work with students and families to 
address the concerns and reinforce expectations. 
 
Committee Member Turner asked for clarification regarding the transportation specialists' 
responsibilities.  Dr. Espinola explained that transportation specialists were responsible for 
dispatching, routing, and providing daily operational support to bus drivers. 
 
Committee Member Turner emphasized that student behavior could directly affect driver

15. NEW BUSINESS  
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell brought forward a concern received from a recently retired 
Manchester School District teacher who had sought to return to the District as a substitute 
teacher.  He explained that the individual had retired at the conclusion of the prior school year 
after approximately 22 years of service and wished to begin substitute teaching in September. 
The former employee expressed frustration upon learning that he would be required to complete 
another criminal background check and personally pay the associated fee, despite having only 
recently retired from the District. 
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell questioned whether the District could consider a different approach 
for longtime employees seeking to return shortly after retirement. 
 
Attorney Upton explained that New Hampshire law required substitute teachers to undergo 
criminal background checks every three years.  He stated that the individual had not undergone a 
new criminal background check during his many years of continuous employment and that 
allowing him to return as a substitute without satisfying the requirement would violate state law. 
Attorney Upton also noted that background check requirements were becoming more extensive 
and that current certified teachers would face additional screening requirements through the 
recertification process. 
 
Vice Chairman O'Connell clarified that he was not requesting an exemption from the background 
check itself but was suggesting that the District consider covering or waiving the associated fee 
for longtime employees returning as substitutes.  Attorney Upton clarified that the actual 
background check fee was $47, rather than the $25 originally referenced. 
 
Dr. Chmiel explained that the fee was paid to an outside entity and that if the District waived the 
charge for an applicant, the District would still be responsible for paying it.  She cautioned that 
providing an exemption to one category of employees could create expectations for similar 
treatment across other employee groups and that the financial and administrative implications 
should be considered.
